questions.scenario: Rookwood Energy's maintenance planner has just read a 30-page boiler inspection report. She asks Claude: 'Read this and tell me whether it's safe to keep running.' The reply runs to about 400 words, walks through every section of the report in order, and closes with one sentence: 'Overall, the unit appears to be functioning within acceptable parameters.' She has ten minutes before shift handover and needs a decision, not a summary.
questions.stem: What is the BEST diagnosis and the BEST change to her request?

options.text: The report is too technical to be judged directly, so she should ask for a plain-English summary first and read her decision out of that.
She is using the wrong feature. This is recurring work on the same standard report type, so it belongs in a Project with the reporting standard held as knowledge.

Nothing in the request says what the answer should look like, so Claude defaulted to summarising the document. Ask for the verdict first, then the single reason, then the specific evidence she should check.
Inspection reasoning is a demanding task, so the change is to rerun it on the most capable model available before she relies on the answer.

questions.explanation: The reply is competent — it is simply the wrong artefact. Nothing in the request specified a shape, so the default was a document summary. The reliable fix is to name the shape: **verdict first, then the reason, then the specific evidence**, and to say what to do if the report does not settle the question. Naming the output format is the single highest-value thing you can add to a request whose answer has to be acted on.

whyWrong.A: A plain-English summary is still a summary. It changes the register, not the shape, so she still has to read the whole thing to find the answer she asked for.
whyWrong.B: Where the work happens is not the problem. She has one report in front of her and one question; nothing here recurs across chats or needs to be shared, so a Project would add ceremony without fixing anything.
whyWrong.D: A more capable model given the same underspecified request will still produce a well-written summary. The gap is between what was asked for and what came back, and that is a property of the request, not of the model.

questions.mindset: A reply that summarises when you asked for a decision is a missing output format, not a missing capability.

questions.scenario: Halcyon Legal's supervising partner runs a case-management meeting every Monday. The paralegal drafts the agenda notes by pasting the week's matters into a chat with the instruction 'Write the meeting notes.' The notes have no headings, no owners against actions and no separation of decisions from discussion, so the partner now retypes them before circulating them to fee-earners.
questions.stem: Which change addresses the root cause of the rework?

options.text: Add the date and the meeting title to the top of the request so the notes can be filed correctly.
State the required structure in the request: which sections to produce, that decisions and discussion are kept apart, and that every action carries an owner and a due date.
Ask for a formal legal register, since the audience is fee-earners who expect conventional wording.
Move this into a Project for the litigation team so the firm's drafting conventions apply automatically.

questions.explanation: The instruction names a task but carries none of the **constraints Claude cannot infer**. A filename header is not the constraint that is costing the partner an hour a week; 'every action has an owner and a due date, decisions separated from discussion' is. Unstated constraints are the most common cause of output that is broadly right and structurally unusable.

whyWrong.A: Filing metadata has nothing to do with the missing structure. The partner is not retyping because the notes lack a date.
whyWrong.C: Register affects word choice, not shape. The complaints are about structure — no headings, no owners, decisions mixed into discussion — and a more formal register leaves all three untouched.
whyWrong.D: A Project is the right home when the same material has to be applied repeatedly by more than one person. Here the constraint belongs in the request, and adding a Project would obscure the real fix.

questions.mindset: If the output is the wrong shape, the missing information is a constraint, not a subject.

questions.scenario: Northgate Logistics' dispatch Project instructions have grown to about 140 lines over two years. They include carrier-specific rules that apply to only two of eleven depots, one retired pilot's formatting preferences, and the same four safety rules written three different ways. Dispatchers report that rules are followed inconsistently, and nobody can say which rule is in force for a given job.
questions.stem: What is the BEST diagnosis and next step?

options.text: Length and repetition are burying the rules that matter. Consolidate into a short ranked instruction set, delete what no longer applies, and record which rule governs which case.
The rules conflict but the instruction set does not say how to resolve conflict. Add one line at the top: 'apply all rules in priority order, most specific first.'
Move the carrier-specific rules into a separate Project per carrier so each depot only ever sees rules that apply to its own work.
Ask Claude to restate the relevant instructions before answering, so the rules in force are visible in every reply.

questions.explanation: This is what an instruction set does when nobody prunes it: it becomes a pile rather than a policy, and the rules that matter end up competing for attention with rules that do not apply to the case in hand. The three things that were true — one rule written three ways, two rules for two depots buried among eleven, one belonging to someone who has left — are all **maintenance failures**, and the fix is to reduce the set and record precedence. A priority line does not help when four copies of the same rule are still competing.

whyWrong.B: Precedence only helps when there is a short, coherent set to prioritise. Four differently-worded copies of one rule plus an obsolete personal preference is not a priority problem, and 'most specific first' would give the retired pilot's formatting preference a real vote.
whyWrong.C: Splitting by carrier is a reasonable redesign in a different organisation. Here the carrier rules are two lines in an otherwise shared instruction set; eleven Projects would multiply the maintenance problem this question is about.
whyWrong.D: Restating instructions before each answer adds length to every reply without removing the conflict, and it cannot resolve four competing versions of the same rule. It also makes the configuration harder to see, not easier.

questions.mindset: An instruction set nobody prunes stops being a policy and becomes a pile; conflict is usually a maintenance symptom.

questions.scenario: Marden & Vale's bid team receives a first-draft tender response whose technical section cites 'Clause 7.4 of the Framework Agreement (2023)'. Nobody can find that clause in the framework agreement the team holds. The draft reads fluently, the citation is formatted exactly like the others, and the surrounding argument is sound.
questions.stem: What is the MOST appropriate response?

options.text: Keep the citation but soften the surrounding wording, since the substance is drawn from the client's own written brief.

Ask Claude to re-check the citation against the document and say so plainly if it cannot find it; then treat every unverifiable figure and reference in the same draft as suspect until a person has read it against the source.
Delete the citation and ask Claude to rewrite the technical section without referring to any document at all, so the risk disappears.
Accept the citation. The draft is internally consistent, the argument around it holds, and the bid team's own reviewers will catch anything that turns out to be wrong.

questions.explanation: A citation that cannot be located is not a formatting problem — it is evidence that at least one specific was composed rather than read. The recovery is twofold: get Claude to re-derive it against the source and **say it cannot find it rather than producing a new plausible reference**, and then treat the rest of the draft as unverified until a person has checked the specifics. A fluent draft is exactly the condition under which a fabricated reference survives review.

whyWrong.A: Hedging the wording around an unlocatable clause leaves the claim in place and signals less confidence about a point that is simply not supported. If the clause does not exist, the surrounding sentence is the problem too.
whyWrong.C: Removing the reference protects against the citation but keeps the underlying claim, which is the part that reached the client. Rewriting without a source does not make the statement true.
whyWrong.D: This is the reasoning that lets a fabricated reference reach a client: the draft looks consistent and a reviewer is assumed to be downstream. Precisely formatted specifics are the hardest thing for a reviewer to doubt and the easiest thing to generate wrongly.

questions.mindset: One specific you cannot locate means the specific was generated, so audit the other specifics before you trust the paragraph.

questions.scenario: Ashgrove Legal's intake clerk asks Claude which of two internal fee arrangements applies to a particular client. Claude answers confidently and names a document. She cannot find that document, so she asks again, adding 'are you sure?'. The second answer is longer, restates the same claim with more detail, and cites the same document.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements about what has just happened are accurate? Choose TWO.

options.text: The second answer adds no evidential weight: a model's confidence and extra detail are not independent corroboration of its own earlier claim.
The document name was probably correct but was mangled in transcription, so she should search for close spelling variants before doubting it.
The right next step is to check the firm's own fee schedule or ask the responsible fee-earner, rather than ask the model again.
Because both answers agree and the second is more detailed, the claim is now well supported and can go into the letter without a human check.

questions.explanation: Pressing a model for certainty frequently produces **more assertion, not more evidence** — the detail is generated from the same prior, not retrieved from a second source. The reliable move is to change where the answer comes from: the firm's own fee schedule or the fee-earner who owns it. Unverifiable specifics are exactly what a second, longer answer fails to resolve, and this is a fee arrangement going into a client letter.

whyWrong.B: It is a reasonable thing to try once, but it treats a specific that has already failed one lookup as probably right. If it cannot be found under any plausible name, the explanation is not clerical, and the fee schedule settles it either way.
whyWrong.D: Two answers from the same system are one piece of evidence, not two. Agreement between them is a property of the system, and the length of the second answer is not evidence of anything.

questions.mindset: Re-asking is not a second source; when a specific fails to verify, change where the answer comes from.

questions.scenario: Kestrel Care's rota Project was set up to draft weekly staff rotas from the clinical cover rules. Over the past year, people have quietly started asking it for holiday-cover calculations, agency-rate checks, bank-holiday announcement drafts and a spreadsheet of overtime liability. Rota drafts have become less reliable and nobody can say when that started.
questions.stem: What is the MOST useful next step?

options.text: Tighten the instructions so that rota drafting always takes precedence in any conversation, so the original job is protected.
Roll the extra jobs into the same Project deliberately, and accept that the outputs will now be more varied and less consistent.
Establish what people are actually asking it for, then decide which jobs belong in this Project, which belong in their own, and which it should stop doing.
Move the clinical cover rules out of knowledge and into each individual request, so nothing stale can be loaded by mistake.

questions.explanation: The configuration has **drifted from the job it was built for**, and the symptom — output getting worse with no change anyone made — is what drift looks like from the inside. The diagnosis is that the Project now has four jobs, three of which it was never set up for, each with its own sources and rules. Naming the actual jobs, then splitting or refusing them deliberately, restores the reliability; tightening the instructions just makes four jobs fight inside one.

whyWrong.A: Adding precedence fights the symptom. The rota drafts are less reliable because the Project is carrying holiday calculations and rate checks, not because rota drafting comes second in a list nobody reads.
whyWrong.B: Accepting four jobs makes the degradation official. Each extra job needs its own sources and its own rules, and none of the three was built for — that is exactly the quiet drift already causing the problem.
whyWrong.D: Relocating the rules into each request would remove stale loads but multiply maintenance across every user, and it does nothing about the three jobs the Project was never configured for.

questions.mindset: When a workflow quietly becomes worse without anyone changing it, the configuration has drifted — name the real jobs before tuning anything.

questions.scenario: Silverbrook Foods' packaging team answers roughly the same 25 questions a week from the label artwork manual and the house claims rules. Each person starts a fresh chat and pastes both documents in. Answers are broadly right but differ between people, and when a claims rule changed last month nobody noticed for a fortnight.
questions.stem: Which change is MOST appropriate, and why?

options.text: Keep pasting the documents each time, but add 'use only these documents and do not use outside knowledge' at the start of every request.
Put the manual and the claims rules into a Project's knowledge, so every chat inside it starts from the same sources and one person can update them for the whole team.
Save both documents as attachments on one experienced colleague's chat and ask the team to message her for the answer.
Move the team onto the most capable model, since the differences between their answers come from reasoning rather than from the sources.

questions.explanation: The variation between people comes from **what each of them managed to paste**, not from how the question was reasoned. A Project stores the sources once so every chat starts with them, keeps them identical across the team, and gives the rules a single owner who can update them in one place — which is what would have surfaced the claims change immediately instead of after a fortnight.

whyWrong.A: A warning against outside knowledge narrows sourcing without fixing the actual difference: two people pasting two documents are still working from two different sets, and the stale-rule problem survives.
whyWrong.C: This concentrates expertise in one person's chats and leaves the sources unversioned, so the claims change still needs chasing. It also makes the most experienced colleague a bottleneck for the whole team.
whyWrong.D: A stronger model cannot correct for missing or stale sources. It will produce a more fluent answer from whatever the person happened to paste, and will do so more confidently.

questions.mindset: When two people get different answers to the same standing question, the sources differ — store them once rather than asking everyone to paste them.

questions.scenario: Northgate Logistics' depot supervisor asked Claude in a chat to write a small interactive page where a supervisor enters two shifts and sees the hours and overtime each person ends up with. Claude wrote the page, but it now sits in the middle of a long conversation, and he has to scroll back to find it and copy it out every time he wants to use it.
questions.stem: What is the BEST explanation and change?

options.text: The page is fine. Copy it into a fresh chat whenever it is needed and carry on from there.

This is a working document meant to exist and be used in its own right, not a reply inside a conversation. Ask Claude to turn it into an artifact so it opens as a standalone, versioned piece of work he can return to.
Tools like this should never be kept, because a saved copy drifts out of date. Ask Claude to rebuild the page from a saved prompt each time.
Put the page into the depot Project's knowledge, so it is loaded automatically at the start of every conversation.

questions.explanation: He built a **thing that gets used repeatedly**, so it should exist as a thing rather than as part of a transcript. An artifact is the feature for standalone content inside a chat: it opens on its own, keeps its own version history as it is edited, and can be published or shared. The distinction matters — a useful tool buried in conversation history is something people stop using, not something they maintain.

whyWrong.A: Copying into a fresh chat throws away the history that makes the page understandable and creates a second copy nobody maintains. It solves retrieval and nothing else.
whyWrong.C: Rebuilding each time is the worst of both: the work of finding and reusing the tool is done again for every use, and no version is ever improved deliberately.
whyWrong.D: Knowledge is for reference material Claude should draw on, not for a tool someone has to operate. Loading the page on every conversation would be noise in every unrelated chat.

questions.mindset: If you will use it again and operate it yourself, it is a document, not a reply — make it one.

questions.scenario: Fenmoor Group's analyst produces a monthly pack for six regional managers. Her instruction is 'Summarise the month and tell us what we should do.' It has grown to 200 words of accumulated one-off requests, three of which contradict each other. The packs are getting longer and less decisive, and two managers have now started asking her what the numbers actually mean.
questions.stem: Two colleagues have proposed changes. Which TWO are well founded? Choose TWO.

options.text: Split the job in two — a factual summary, then recommended actions — and ask for them in that order, so each can be judged on its own.
Cap the answer at 300 words, which forces Claude to prioritise and will make the packs more decisive.
Clear the instruction set entirely and rebuild it from a blank Project, in case something in the accumulated history is corrupting the output.
Decide what a good pack looks like by taking the two most useful past packs as worked examples, and replace the accumulated instructions with the specific rules those examples demonstrate.

questions.explanation: Two separate faults, two separate fixes. The request fuses **two different jobs** — report the facts and recommend a course of action — which cannot both be judged when they arrive as one undifferentiated block; asking for them in order makes the first checkable before the second is trusted. And a 200-word instruction set containing three contradictions has no recoverable structure, so the reliable replacement is demonstrated rather than described: the rules that produced the two packs the managers liked.

whyWrong.B: A word cap makes an unfocused answer shorter, not clearer. The problem is that the pack has no shape and no precedence between its rules; compressing it preserves the ambiguity at a smaller size.
whyWrong.C: Clearing the configuration throws away whatever has been learned, and it is not the likeliest cause. Contradicting instructions explain inconsistent packs directly, and rebuilding first means rebuilding the same contradictions from scratch unless the real rules are identified.

questions.mindset: When a request is both fused and over-written, split the jobs and demonstrate the rules rather than describing them.

questions.scenario: Torrington Water's communications team sends a weekly 'what has changed' note to about 900 staff. Three people have emailed feedback this month: one wants shorter sentences, one wants more detail on outages, and one says the notes are 'fine'. Two of the three rarely read the note.
questions.stem: What is the BEST way to use this feedback?

options.text: Apply all three changes, since feedback should be acted on quickly.
Leave the note unchanged, since it is already working and the feedback is too mixed to act on.
Rewrite the note from scratch around what the two respondents who read it want.

Treat the feedback as something to test rather than something to obey: take the last eight weeks of real notes, agree with the people who read them what good looks like, and change one thing at a time against that set.

questions.explanation: The feedback is not wrong, it is untestable: three opinions from people with different relationships to the note cannot be resolved by picking one. What makes feedback actionable is **a set of real cases and an agreed definition of good**, so a change can be shown to help or hurt. Using the last eight weeks gives that set for free, and changing one thing at a time means you can tell which change did what.

whyWrong.A: Acting on all three produces a different note every week and teaches nobody whether any of it worked. It also implements the wishes of two people who do not read the output.
whyWrong.B: Mixed feedback is a normal state. Declining to act leaves the team unable to tell whether the note is fine or simply unexamined, and the outage-detail request in particular sounds like a real gap.
whyWrong.C: Two of three respondents is not a mandate, and one of them asked for less detail while the other asked for more. Rebuilding around them picks winners without evidence.

questions.mindset: Feedback becomes usable when you can measure it: agree what good looks like, then change one thing against real examples.

questions.scenario: Ivybridge College's MIS team exports exam results each term as a spreadsheet in which year groups are merged cells, three columns hold mixed text and numbers, and the class codes are only explained in a separate key document. Claude's summary is well organised, but the per-class numbers are wrong roughly a third of the time and an analyst retypes the correct figures afterwards.
questions.stem: Which change would MOST reduce that rework?

options.text: Ask for the term's export to be produced unmerged, one row per student, with each column either purely numeric or purely text, and the class codes in a column of their own.
Add more detail to the prompt, specifying that merged cells must be handled correctly and that class codes must be looked up in the key document.
Ask Claude to re-read the spreadsheet immediately before producing each summary and to state the source cell for every figure it reports.
Upload the term's export into the Project's knowledge so that every chat can reach it.

questions.explanation: The error rate is a property of the **source material**, not of the prompt. Merged cells, mixed-type columns and codes documented elsewhere all push a one-third failure rate into every prompt you write, and no amount of instruction wording removes them. Asking the MIS team for a clean export — unmerged, one row per student, single-typed columns, codes in their own column — is a small request that removes the failure mode entirely, and it is cheaper than the manual correction it replaces.

whyWrong.B: Telling a model to handle merged cells correctly asks it to compensate for a defect in the file. It will be right most of the time and wrong in a way nobody can predict, which is worse than a consistent shape.
whyWrong.C: Requiring a source cell for each figure improves traceability and would let you catch errors faster. It does not remove the errors, and the analyst still retypes them.
whyWrong.D: Storing the messy export in knowledge makes it available but leaves it just as ambiguous, and it adds a copy that can go stale without anyone noticing.

questions.mindset: When rework comes from the shape of the input, fix the input — no prompt wording removes a defect in the source.

questions.scenario: Redhaven Renewables' project office turns site-meeting voice recordings into decision logs. A contractor's own notes are inconsistent about who committed to what, so Claude's logs disagree with the contractor's record and the project office now keeps both and reconciles them by hand.
questions.stem: Which change would MOST reduce that hand reconciliation?

options.text: Ask Claude to mark any commitment it cannot attribute to a named speaker as 'unattributed', so the disagreements are visible rather than asserted.
Have the recordings transcribed with speaker labels before they reach Claude, so the source itself names who said what.
Instruct Claude to prefer the contractor's written notes wherever the two differ, since the written record is the official one.
Ask Claude to produce both versions side by side with a recommended reading, and let the project office choose between them each week.

questions.explanation: Reconciliation is happening because the **source does not say who said what**. Getting speaker-labelled transcription puts that into the material once, and every downstream log, summary and handover inherits it. This is the same move as asking MIS for a clean export: the disagreement is not a reasoning failure that prompting can talk Claude out of.

whyWrong.A: Flagging unattributed commitments is a reasonable safeguard and would surface some ambiguity honestly, but it still leaves the project office doing the reconciliation by hand. It manages the symptom at the point of output instead of fixing the input.
whyWrong.C: Preferring one record removes the disagreement by decree. Where the two genuinely differ, the wrong one wins by default and the project office loses the signal that there is a dispute to resolve.
whyWrong.D: Two versions plus a recommendation is a bigger reconciliation task than the one it replaces, and it puts the judgement back on the person doing the most work.

questions.mindset: If people are reconciling outputs, the source is missing information the task needs — fix the source once.

questions.scenario: Fernwood Legal's paralegal has revised the same intake-summary prompt five times in three weeks. Each version scores slightly better on the cases she has tried, but the remaining failures never change: the summary is wrong whenever an enquiry describes two separate matters in one email. Six colleagues now spend about ten extra minutes a case correcting it.
questions.stem: What is the BEST judgement here?

options.text: Keep iterating, because each revision has improved something measurable and stopping would waste the work done so far.
Rewrite the instruction from scratch without reference to the current version, in case it has become tangled during the five rounds of changes.
Stop tuning the prompt. The failures are a property of the input — one enquiry containing two matters — so change the step that produces the material, or handle each enquiry separately.
Escalate to the firm's software vendor, since the model has now shown it cannot be relied on for legal intake work.

questions.explanation: Five revisions have moved the average and left the failure mode **exactly where it was**, which is the signal that the prompt is not the variable. One email describing two matters is a genuine ambiguity in the material, and no instruction reliably resolves it — which is why the same cases fail every time. The remaining two levers are upstream: split the enquiry at intake, or have the summary explicitly state which matter it covers so a person can see the gap.

whyWrong.A: The premise is wrong: the residual failures did not improve. Six colleagues paying ten minutes a case for no movement in the failure set is a cost with no return, and each further round is another round.
whyWrong.B: A clean rewrite discards working behaviour and re-encounters the same ambiguous cases. Nothing in the history indicates the instruction has become tangled — the failures are all of one type.
whyWrong.D: This presents a specific input problem as a verdict on the tool. Six colleagues get useful output on the great majority of matters; the fix is upstream of the model.

questions.mindset: When several revisions move the average but not the failure set, the failure lives in the input, not the prompt.

questions.scenario: Arikon Freight's operations team has spent two weeks improving the prompt behind customer-facing delivery-status emails. Complaints have fallen and the emails are measurably better. They have also run two further rounds of tweaks aimed at a stubborn 3% of cases, and the person who built the workflow has now left the company.
questions.stem: What is the MOST defensible decision?

options.text: Continue, because the improvements are real and abandoning a working customer-facing workflow is worse than living with a small imperfection.
Stop and rebuild from scratch, since two weeks of undocumented refinement cannot be trusted to have been an improvement.
Make the decision explicit and record it: keep the current version with its known failure rate documented and assigned to a named owner, rather than continuing to tune it or rebuilding it.
Keep the prompt for internal drafts but stop using it for customer emails until the failure rate reaches zero.

questions.explanation: Abandoning is not the only alternative to persisting. The defensible move is to **stop optimising and take ownership**: state the known failure rate, say which cases cause it, and put a named person in charge of it. That converts an undocumented 3% risk into a managed one, and it survives the person who built it leaving — which nothing about the current arrangement does.

whyWrong.A: Persisting without naming the residual risk just extends an undocumented problem. Two rounds on the same 3% has already stopped paying, and the owner has left.
whyWrong.B: Rebuilding discards a workflow with measured results — complaints fell — and produces a second untested version during a period when nobody owns the original.
whyWrong.D: Refusing to use it for customers at a 3% failure rate discards most of the benefit. The right response to a small known failure rate is a documented one with an owner, not withdrawal.

questions.mindset: When a workflow is good but not perfect, the choice is not keep-tuning or rebuild — it is documenting the residual risk and naming an owner.

questions.scenario: Riverton Credit Union's complaints team uses Claude to draft replies to customer complaints. The drafts are consistently courteous and consistently miss the point of the complaint, because each reply is drafted from the whole complaint thread at once. The team's own data shows that complaints about the same three issues go unresolved most often.
questions.stem: Which change is MOST likely to help?

options.text: Ask for a longer, warmer reply, since tone is what customers respond to and the messages are already polite.
Move the drafting to a more capable model, since identifying what a customer actually wants is a reasoning problem.
Split the job: first have Claude state the customer's actual issue and the outcome they want in one line, have a person check that line against the complaint, and only then draft the reply.
Add the three most common complaint types to the Project instructions as worked examples.

questions.explanation: The failure is **upstream of the prose**: the complaint is never reduced to its actual issue and desired outcome before the reply is written. Splitting the work creates a checkpoint on exactly that step, and it is cheap — one line to review instead of a paragraph. The pattern is the general one: when a long intermediate product is reliably wrong, insert a short intermediate product you can check.

whyWrong.A: The drafts are already courteous, so tone is not the reported problem. Adding warmth lengthens replies that already fail to address the complaint.
whyWrong.B: A more capable model reading the same thread in one pass will produce a more fluent response to the wrong target. The missing step is the single-line extraction, not the capability.
whyWrong.D: Examples of complaint types would help classification, but the reply is drafted from the whole thread, so the model is never asked to classify anything before it writes.

questions.mindset: When a long output is reliably wrong, insert a short intermediate output you can check before the writing starts.

questions.scenario: Calder & Sons' estimating team has a prompt that has produced good quotes reliably for a year. A new surveyor wants one new requirement: every quote must name the scaffolding type it has assumed and flag the cases where no site photo exists. Two change proposals are on the table.
questions.stem: Which TWO approaches best protect what already works? Choose TWO.

options.text: Change the prompt, then re-test it against the last 30 quotes before it goes back into use.
Change it in the team chat, where every surveyor can see the discussion and the reason behind the new rule.
Leave the estimating prompt alone and make the new requirement an explicit step the surveyor completes after the draft quote returns.
Rewrite the whole prompt to include the new requirement, then ask the team to check the first ten quotes by eye.

questions.explanation: A year of reliable output is an asset with no test suite behind it, so any change needs **evidence before it becomes the default**. Re-testing against the last 30 real quotes is cheap and reuses work the team already has. And the new requirement does not have to live inside the prompt at all — as an explicit step after the draft, it is visible, reviewable and reversible, and it leaves a prompt that has been working for a year working.

whyWrong.B: Making the change where the discussion happens builds no evidence. It also puts the rule somewhere nobody looks when a quote is wrong, so the next failure arrives without the context that explains it.
whyWrong.D: Rewriting the whole prompt to add one requirement risks the behaviour that has held for a year, and eyeballing ten quotes is not a regression check — it is a sample nobody agreed was representative.

questions.mindset: A working prompt has no test suite, so any change needs evidence against past real cases before it becomes the default.

questions.scenario: Marden & Vale's bid team answers the same 40 due-diligence questions for every new supplier, drawing on the same internal documents. Each bid manager starts a fresh chat, re-pastes the compliance policy, the insurance requirements and the previous answers, and then copies the finished answers into the bid document.
questions.stem: Where is the avoidable waste, and what removes most of it?

options.text: In the length of the answers, so ask for shorter replies.

In re-establishing and re-transcribing the same answers for every bid. Put the 40 questions, the source documents and the approved answers in a Project, so each bid supplies only the new supplier's facts.
In the size of the due-diligence list, which should be cut to the ten questions that matter most.
In the copying step, which should be handed to one person who copies all answers in for the team.

questions.explanation: The waste is **re-establishing standing content**. The questions, the source documents and the previously approved answers are identical for every bid; only the supplier's own facts change. A Project holds the standing content once, applies it automatically to every chat, and — because there is a single copy — keeps the approved answers current instead of letting each bid manager's pasted copy drift. It also removes the copy-out step, because the answers are already in the chat in the right form.

whyWrong.A: Brevity is not the cost. The time goes into finding, pasting, re-establishing and copying content that does not change from bid to bid.
whyWrong.C: The 40 questions are the firm's due diligence. Cutting them reduces the work being done rather than the waste in doing it.
whyWrong.D: Handing the copying to one person keeps the re-establishment work in place and creates a new single point of failure and a new queue.

questions.mindset: If the same material is retyped into every conversation, store it once where it applies automatically.

questions.scenario: Rookwood Energy's project office asks Claude to draft the same three-paragraph executive update for each of nine live projects. Each update is decent, but they read inconsistently from one month to the next, because every project manager types the facts in a different order and uses different wording for the same things — availability, outage, constraint.
questions.stem: Which change would MOST improve the work, and why?

options.text: Ask every project manager to supply the facts in a fixed order under fixed headings, so the updates come back in one house shape and month-to-month comparison across projects becomes possible.
Have one manager produce all nine updates, so the style is consistent by construction.
Add one example of an ideal update to the Project instructions and leave the way people type their facts as it is.
Create a separate Project per project, each with instructions tailored to that asset.

questions.explanation: Standardising the input is the cheapest way to standardise the output. A fixed order and fixed headings give the model a consistent structure to work from **and** make the nine updates genuinely comparable, which is most of what executives want from a nine-project summary. It costs one agreed form rather than nine separate configurations.

whyWrong.B: Consistency by one author is consistency for that author's month. It also creates a single point of failure for the whole estate and scales to nine projects only by adding people.
whyWrong.C: An example shows the shape of the answer but not the shape of the input, so each manager's differently-ordered facts still produce differently-structured updates.
whyWrong.D: Nine tailored Projects means nine instruction sets to maintain and no shared comparison basis, which is the thing the executives were missing.

questions.mindset: Standardising the input is usually cheaper and more effective than standardising the output after the fact.

questions.scenario: Kestrel Care's governance team has Claude summarise inspection findings into corrective-action plans. Each plan then takes about 25 minutes of manual work: someone has to assign an owner from a rota the model has never seen, and set a date around a leave calendar it does not know either.
questions.stem: Which TWO changes would MOST remove that manual work? Choose TWO.

options.text: Ask for shorter corrective-action plans, which reduces the amount of editing a person has to do.
Make the current owner rota and the leave calendar part of the Project's knowledge, so plans can be assigned and dated against real constraints.
Add the owners and target dates as fields on the inspection form the inspector already completes, so the material arrives with the findings.
Ask Claude to suggest an owner and a date anyway and have a person confirm them at the end, so at least the suggestion is there to start from.

questions.explanation: Both changes supply information the task needs **before** the model has to invent it. The rota and leave calendar as knowledge makes assignment and dating possible in one pass and stays current because the rota team maintains it. Capturing owner and date on the form the inspector already fills in is even better for this particular gap: the person with the knowledge supplies it once, at the moment they have it, and the manual step disappears entirely.

whyWrong.A: Shorter plans do not create owners. The 25 minutes is spent on scheduling decisions, which get harder to make from a thinner document, not easier.
whyWrong.D: A suggestion without the rota behind it is a guess, and a person confirming it has to do the same check the assignment did. It moves the work rather than removing it.

questions.mindset: Manual work after the draft is usually missing input, not missing effort — supply the rota and the dates at the source.

questions.scenario: Northgate Logistics changed its dispatch Project's instructions and the model tier at the same time to cut cost, and monthly spend fell by half. Nobody recorded what the output looked like before the change, so depot managers now say the notes are 'a bit vaguer' but nobody can demonstrate it — and the change is being extended to two more depots.
questions.stem: Which TWO actions are MOST appropriate before extending the change? Choose TWO.

options.text: Revert immediately and return to the previous configuration, because a change that cannot be evidenced should not be kept.
Assemble a set of recent real dispatch notes alongside the previous versions of them, and check the new output against that set.
Collect the depot managers' detailed impressions of where the new notes are less useful, since they are the people the notes serve.
Extend it to the two depots now so more data accumulates faster, and review properly after three months.

questions.explanation: The honest position is that the change is **unevidenced**, and two kinds of evidence are available and complementary. Comparing new output against real past notes shows whether quality moved. Asking the depot managers where the new notes are less useful turns an unfalsifiable 'a bit vaguer' into specific, fixable complaints — and those users are the only people who know what the notes are for. Only after both can the rollout decision be made on evidence.

whyWrong.A: Reverting on no evidence discards a change that halved cost, on the strength of an impression nobody can substantiate. That is the same error in the opposite direction.
whyWrong.D: Rolling out to more depots before establishing whether quality held extends an unmeasured change and makes it harder to attribute any future problem to this decision.

questions.mindset: An unmeasured optimisation is not an optimisation — build the evidence from real past outputs and from the people who use them.

questions.scenario: Silverbrook Foods' claims team shortened its Claude-assisted first-notification letters to save handling time. Response times improved. Six weeks later, three recipients have written to say the letters did not explain how to appeal, and the regulator's guidance is explicit that appeal rights must appear in the first notification.
questions.stem: What is the BEST reading of what happened?

options.text: A required element fell out when the letters were shortened, so appeal information needs to be restored as an explicit, checked requirement rather than left to the draft.
Three complaints out of hundreds is within a normal range, and the evidence does not support further structural change.
The recipients were confused by the shorter letters, so the fix is more neutral wording rather than more length.
The regulator's guidance may be out of date, so legal should confirm it before anyone changes the letters.

questions.explanation: An optimisation that removed a **required** element is not a successful optimisation, whatever it did to handling time. Appeal rights are a compliance requirement, and they are now an emergent property of a long draft rather than a checked step. The correction is to state the requirement explicitly and verify it per letter — for example by asking for the appeal paragraph as a distinct, named element that cannot be dropped when someone asks for a shorter letter.

whyWrong.B: That reasoning works for taste complaints and not for regulatory ones. Three complaints are irrelevant if each one is a breach of an explicit requirement.
whyWrong.C: Wording is not the issue. The appeal information is absent, not phrased badly, and adding neutral words will not put it back.
whyWrong.D: Whether the guidance is current is worth a check, but it does not explain three letters missing a required element, and checking it is not a substitute for putting the requirement back in as something you verify.

questions.mindset: If an efficiency change removed something required, restore it as an explicit checkable requirement — speed never outranks compliance.

questions.scenario: Fernwood Legal's operations manager has watched colleagues spend time re-checking Claude's intake summaries, and has designed an 'optimised' workflow: one person reviews a batch of 25 summaries at the end of each day and corrects them in bulk, with nobody reviewing anything before that. She now proposes extending the same pattern to Claude-drafted first-response emails.
questions.stem: Which TWO concerns should she resolve before adopting this? Choose TWO.

options.text: Bulk correction at the end of the day means errors reach clients before anyone sees them, and these are the firm's first response to people who may already be distressed.
Reviewing once a day is less frequent than current practice, and review frequency should only ever increase over time.
One person cannot check 25 matters a day to the standard the firm applies to intake, so the capacity and the scope of each review need sizing before the design is adopted.
The design makes the operations manager personally responsible for everything the Project sends, which is a legal exposure she should decline.

questions.explanation: Both concerns are about **whether the review can actually do its job**. Batching to the end of the day moves the first check behind the point of no return for a client who has just complained about something urgent. And the design has to be sized: one person reviewing 25 intake matters a day is a throughput assumption, not a fact, and intake review is exactly where a miss does the most damage. Both need answering with evidence before the pattern extends to email.

whyWrong.B: The principle is wrong. Review frequency is not monotonic — what matters is that a check happens before a message reaches someone, and some checks belong earlier than others for reasons of urgency, not of trend.
whyWrong.D: The design would make her responsible for the workflow's outputs in the ordinary sense of owning a process, which is normal managerial accountability. The real issues are timing and capacity, not personal liability.

questions.mindset: Before batching a review to save time, check that the review still happens before the message reaches the person it affects, and that one person can do it.
